title: Basic Economic Concepts
subtitle: The formulas, ideas, and traps you actually need for Basic Economic Concepts.
objectives: Apply scarcity, opportunity cost, and the PPC.
Use comparative advantage and gains from trade.
Read PPC shifts as growth.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: The value of the next-best alternative given up.
Lower opportunity cost; the basis for gains from trade.
On the curve = efficient; inside = unemployment; outside = unattainable; outward shift = growth.
Land, labor, capital, entrepreneurship (money is NOT a factor).

traps: Trade gains come from comparative (not absolute) advantage.
sections.example: If a worker earning $30/hr takes an hour off, the opportunity cost is $30.

Distinguish nominal and real values.
Identify business-cycle phases.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: C + I + G + Xn.
unemployed ÷ labor force × 100.
Real is inflation-adjusted; real GDP growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation.
(CPI₂ − CPI₁)/CPI₁ × 100.

sections.example: Labor force 150M, 9M unemployed → 9/150 = 6%.

title: National Income & Price Determination
subtitle: The formulas, ideas, and traps you actually need for National Income & Price Determination.
objectives: Use AD/AS to find equilibrium.
Apply the spending and tax multipliers.
Distinguish recessionary and inflationary gaps.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: −MPC/(1 − MPC) (smaller in magnitude than the spending multiplier).
Output below full employment; close with expansionary policy.
Vertical at potential output; only growth shifts it.

traps: A demand shift moves output and price level the same direction; a supply shift moves them opposite.
sections.example: MPC 0.8 → multiplier 1/(1−0.8) = 5; a $50B spending rise can raise GDP up to $250B.

Use the money multiplier.
Connect the Fed's tools to interest rates.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: 1 ÷ reserve requirement.
Fed buys bonds → money supply up, rates down; sells bonds → opposite.
Downward-sloping vs. the interest rate; more real GDP shifts it right.
Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value.

traps: Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions.
sections.example: Reserve requirement 25% → money multiplier = 1/0.25 = 4.

title: Stabilization & Long-Run Policy
subtitle: The formulas, ideas, and traps you actually need for Stabilization & Long-Run Policy.
objectives: Choose fiscal and monetary policy for the goal.
Explain growth and the long-run self-correction.
Recognize policy lags and crowding out.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Cut taxes / raise spending, or buy bonds / lower rates — fights recession.
Raise taxes / cut spending, or sell bonds / raise rates — fights inflation.
Rightward LRAS shift from more resources, capital, or technology.
Government borrowing raises rates and reduces private investment.

traps: Money is neutral in the long run — sustained money growth raises prices, not real output.
sections.example: To fight a recession: cut taxes / increase G (fiscal) or buy bonds / lower rates (monetary).

title: Open Economy: Trade & Finance
subtitle: The formulas, ideas, and traps you actually need for Open Economy: Trade & Finance.
objectives: Read the balance of payments.
Explain floating exchange rates.
Link interest rates to capital flows and currency value.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Exports − imports.
The price of one currency in another; set by supply and demand (floating).
Higher demand for a currency raises its value, making exports pricier abroad.
Higher domestic interest rates attract foreign investment, appreciating the currency.

traps: A stronger (appreciated) currency tends to reduce net exports.
sections.example: Rising exports raise demand for the currency → it appreciates.

title: Basic Economic Concepts
subtitle: The formulas, ideas, and traps you actually need for Basic Economic Concepts.
objectives: Apply scarcity, opportunity cost, marginal analysis.
Use the PPC and comparative advantage.
Separate positive from normative claims.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Act while marginal benefit ≥ marginal cost.
The next-best alternative forgone.
Lower opportunity cost; drives specialization and trade.
Positive = testable fact; normative = value judgment ('should').

traps: Sunk costs are irrelevant to decisions — only marginal costs and benefits matter.
sections.example: Diminishing marginal utility is why demand curves slope downward.

title: Supply & Demand
subtitle: The formulas, ideas, and traps you actually need for Supply & Demand.
objectives: Shift vs. move along curves.
Compute and apply elasticity.
Analyze price controls, taxes, and surplus.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: %ΔQ / %ΔP; |E| < 1 inelastic, > 1 elastic.
Inelastic: price↑ raises revenue. Elastic: price↑ lowers revenue.
Binding ceiling (below eq.) → shortage; binding floor (above eq.) → surplus.
Falls more on the more inelastic side of the market.

traps: A binding price ceiling causes a shortage, not a surplus.
sections.example: Elasticity 0.5 (inelastic): raising price increases total revenue.

title: Production, Cost & Perfect Competition
subtitle: The formulas, ideas, and traps you actually need for Production, Cost & Perfect Competition.
objectives: Distinguish fixed, variable, marginal, and average costs.
Apply the profit-max and shutdown rules.
Describe long-run competitive equilibrium.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Produce where MR = MC; for a price taker, P = MR.
Operate short-run only if price ≥ minimum AVC.
Total cost ÷ quantity; MC crosses ATC at its minimum.
P = min ATC, zero economic (but normal) profit.

traps: Zero economic profit ≠ losing money — it means a normal return covering opportunity cost.
sections.example: Profit = (P − ATC)×Q: 100 units at $15 with ATC $10 → $500.

title: Imperfect Competition
subtitle: The formulas, ideas, and traps you actually need for Imperfect Competition.
objectives: Compare monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition.
Explain why MR < P for a monopolist.
Use basic game theory.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Higher price, lower output, deadweight loss vs. competition.
A monopolist must lower price on all units to sell more, so MR is below price.
Needs market power and the ability to prevent resale.
Each firm's dominant strategy yields a worse joint outcome than cooperation.

traps: For a competitive firm P = MR; for a monopolist MR < P — don't mix them up.
sections.example: Perfect price discrimination captures all consumer surplus and removes deadweight loss.

title: Factor Markets
subtitle: The formulas, ideas, and traps you actually need for Factor Markets.
objectives: Derive labor demand from marginal revenue product.
Find the cost-minimizing input mix.
Explain wage determination.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: MRP = marginal product × price; hire while MRP ≥ wage.
Equalize marginal product per dollar across inputs.
Demand for labor comes from demand for the output it makes.
A single buyer of labor pays below the competitive wage and hires fewer workers.

traps: Labor demand is 'derived' — it depends on the value of what labor produces.
sections.example: Marginal product 10, output price $5 → MRP = $50; hire while wage ≤ $50.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Overproduction; correct with a Pigouvian tax equal to the external cost.
Underproduction; correct with a subsidy equal to the external benefit.
Non-rival and non-excludable → underprovided due to free riders.
Lost total surplus from mutually beneficial trades that don't occur.

traps: Common resources (rival, non-excludable) are overused — the tragedy of the commons.
sections.example: Consumer surplus = ½ × base × height of the triangle below demand, above price.
